title: How do you index JSON fields (`CREATE INDEX idx ON tbl USING GIN (data jsonb_path_ops)`) and query them efficiently (`WHERE data @> '{"status": "active"}'`)?
shortTitle: How to index and efficiently query JSON fields

s1_definition.profdef: You index jsonb with a GIN index, which stores every key/value path so containment and existence queries can be answered without scanning. The `jsonb_path_ops` operator class makes a smaller, faster index that supports the containment operator `@>`. For queries on a single scalar key you can instead build a b-tree expression index on the extracted value. Efficient querying then uses `@>` containment for the GIN path or an equality on the expression for the b-tree path.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India stores flexible KYC in jsonb. Without an index, finding "all active customers" reads every document. A GIN index is like a cross-reference catalogue of every field and value in those documents, so the bank jumps straight to the active ones. If the bank only ever searches by one field, a focused b-tree index on just that field is even leaner.
s1_definition.oneliner: GIN with jsonb_path_ops for containment queries; a b-tree expression index for a single hot scalar key.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You index jsonb with a GIN index, which stores every key/value path so containment and existence queries can be answered without scanning. The `jsonb_path_ops` operator class makes a smaller, faster index that supports the containment operator `@>`. For queries on a single scalar key you can instead build a b-tree expression index on the extracted value. Efficient querying then uses `@>` containment for the GIN path or an equality on the expression for the b-tree path.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India stores flexible KYC in jsonb. Without an index, finding "all active customers" reads every document. A GIN index is like a cross-reference catalogue of every field and value in those documents, so the bank jumps straight to the active ones. If the bank only ever searches by one field, a focused b-tree index on just that field is even leaner.

**One line to remember:** GIN with jsonb_path_ops for containment queries; a b-tree expression index for a single hot scalar key.

sections.s2_technical:
A default GIN index `USING GIN (data)` indexes keys and values and supports containment `@>`, existence `?`, and path operators. `USING GIN (data jsonb_path_ops)` indexes only the value paths needed for containment, producing a smaller, faster index that supports `@>` but not the key-existence operator. Query it with `WHERE data @> '{"status":"active"}'`, which means "the document contains this sub-object," and the planner can use the GIN index.

If you only ever filter on one scalar, a b-tree expression index is better: `CREATE INDEX ON customers ((kyc->>'status'))` then `WHERE kyc->>'status' = 'active'` becomes a normal index seek and also supports ordering and ranges. In PostgreSQL 12+ you can additionally index JSONPath with GIN for `@?` and `@@`.

Senior nuance: GIN indexes are larger and slower to update than b-tree, so weigh write cost. Match the index to the query operator exactly — a GIN on the whole document does not speed up `kyc->>'status' = 'active'` (that needs the expression index), and a b-tree expression index does not help a containment query. Always confirm with EXPLAIN that the intended index is chosen.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's compliance screen filters customers by KYC status over millions of rows and it scans every document. This is exactly what a JSON index fixes: a GIN index for containment or a b-tree expression index for the single status key.

The demo has an `IndexedKycStore` that builds two in-memory "indexes" — a containment map (GIN analogue) and a value map (b-tree expression analogue) — and shows both answer the active-status query with a direct lookup for Rajesh and Priya.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
kyc-index-service/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/java/com/bank/jsonidx/
    ├── IndexDemo.java
    ├── model/Customer.java
    └── service/IndexedKycStore.java
```

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__kyc_index.sql (PostgreSQL)
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id   VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    kyc  JSONB NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES
 ('SAV2001','Rajesh Kumar','{"status":"active","city":"Delhi"}'),
 ('CUR3001','Priya Sharma','{"status":"pending","city":"Delhi"}');

-- Option A: GIN with jsonb_path_ops → supports containment @>
CREATE INDEX idx_kyc_path ON customers USING GIN (kyc jsonb_path_ops);
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM customers WHERE kyc @> '{"status":"active"}';  -- Bitmap Index Scan on idx_kyc_path

-- Option B: b-tree expression index → supports equality/range/order on one key
CREATE INDEX idx_kyc_status ON customers ((kyc->>'status'));
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM customers WHERE kyc->>'status' = 'active';     -- Index Scan on idx_kyc_status
```

```yaml

spring:
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: two customers, Rajesh (status active) and Priya (status pending), with a GIN-style index and a b-tree-style status index built at load time.

Step 1: byContainment("status","active") looks up the token "status=active" in the GIN analogue and returns SAV2001 directly — no scan.

Step 2: byStatus("active") looks up the status value in the b-tree analogue and also returns SAV2001.

Step 3: Both return the same id, each via its matching index operator.

```text
2026-10-25 18:26:00 [INFO] GIN @> {status:active} -> [SAV2001]
containment -> [SAV2001]
2026-10-25 18:26:00 [INFO] btree status=active -> [SAV2001]
btree       -> [SAV2001]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  query: active customers
    │
    ├─ kyc @> '{"status":"active"}'   → GIN (jsonb_path_ops) → [SAV2001]
    └─ kyc->>'status' = 'active'      → b-tree expression idx → [SAV2001]
    ▼
  result ids (no full document scan)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — IndexedKycStore ═══

  ┌─ Choice: GIN jsonb_path_ops (containment) vs b-tree expr (one key) ─┐
  │  SOLID S: store answers key/value lookups only                      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │       IndexedKycStore        │
  │  - ginIndex: Map<tok,Set>    │  @> containment
  │  - statusIndex: Map<val,Set> │  ->> equality/range
  │  + byContainment(k,v): Set   │
  │  + byStatus(s): Set          │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Rule: index must match the query operator; verify with EXPLAIN.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To index JSON efficiently in PostgreSQL I use a GIN index on the jsonb column, and when my access pattern is containment I add the jsonb_path_ops operator class, which indexes only the value paths needed for the containment operator and produces a smaller, faster index. I then query with the at-greater-than containment operator, asking whether the document contains a given sub-object, and the planner uses the GIN index instead of scanning. When the access pattern is always a single scalar key, I prefer a b-tree expression index on the extracted value, because that supports equality, ranges, and ordering as a normal index seek.

In our National Bank of India compliance screen that filters customers by KYC status over millions of rows, the unindexed query scanned every document. I added a GIN index with jsonb_path_ops so the active-customer filter using containment became an index scan, and for the hot status key I also created a b-tree expression index on the extracted status so a plain equality filter is a direct seek. The key discipline is that the index must match the query operator exactly — a GIN on the whole document does not accelerate an extracted-text equality, and a b-tree expression index does not help a containment query — and I always confirm the chosen plan with EXPLAIN, remembering that GIN indexes cost more on writes. The line I remember is: GIN with jsonb_path_ops for containment, and a b-tree expression index for a single hot scalar key.

---

keyPoints: Index: data structure for fast lookup — B-tree most common
Speeds up WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY — slows down INSERT/UPDATE
Composite index: left-prefix rule — order matters
Covering index: all query columns in index — no table lookup needed
